title: Hope
hook: hope that is seen is not hope (Romans 8:24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, disasters: the tower in Siloam, mercies new every morning, and Nehemiah's let us rise up and build. Your line was rebuild. Did you give the gift you chose? Day one thousand four hundred seven.

These have been heavy days. Failure. Growing old. A child's death. How long, O Lord. War. Floods and earthquakes. One hard room after another. And now, at the end of it, one word that Christians set against all of it. Not as a bandage. As a direction. Paul wrote about it in a letter to the Christians in Rome, and he defined it in a way that sounds, at first, almost like a riddle: hope that is seen is not hope. Today: hope.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here is the riddle in full, in the King James words: "For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it." It's simple once you hear it. Nobody hopes for the sunrise once the sun is up. You only hope for what isn't here yet. So hope, in Paul's sense, isn't a mood that comes when things look good. It's what you hold when things don't. And look at where Paul says this. A few lines earlier he describes the whole world in pain: "For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now." Travaileth: the old word for labor, for giving birth. Paul doesn't pretend the groaning isn't real. He hears it as labor pains. Painful, yes. But pain that is going somewhere. That is the shape of hope in this chapter. It is not optimism, the guess that things will probably work out. In Paul's letter it is trust in a promise that God will finish what he started, and for Christians the resurrection of Jesus is the first sign of it. Paul uses Abraham as the example. Abraham, he says, "against hope believed in hope." Against all the evidence, he kept hoping. And the letter to the Hebrews ties hope to faith: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." Things not seen. In Paul's letter, every one of those hard rooms has that unseen thing at the far end. Not a door anyone can see yet. A door Christians trust is there.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hope for something unseen. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last few days: failure, age, grief, injustice, war, disaster. Choose the one that stayed with you most. Now name one thing you hope for in it, something you cannot see yet. A healing. A reconciliation. A peace. Don't argue with yourself about how likely it is. Just hold it, the way you'd hold a seed in a closed hand. If you pray, you can offer it to God in Paul's words, that we hope for that we see not. The bell holds the time.
Hope. In Paul's letter, the trust that holds on to what isn't seen yet, the way a woman in labor holds on to a child she hasn't met.
Your line: hope unseen. Today, when something looks finished, stuck or broken, say quietly, not yet. Then keep the thing you hope for in view. Day one thousand four hundred seven.

howItsDone: Christians speak of hope in the resurrection at funerals, in the creeds and in prayers for the sick and the dying, and churches mark it each year at Easter and in the waiting season of Advent.

fork.setup: you're Paul, writing to Rome. the whole creation is groaning in pain. how do you describe that pain?
options: as punishment that will never end.
as labor pains, pain that is going somewhere.
as an illusion to be ignored.
fork.reveal: Paul says the creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together: the word for labor. the pain is real, and it is heading toward a birth.

original.note: Greek: hope — the word in Romans 8:24.

trapdoor: what you thought: hope means feeling sure things will be fine.
what it means: in Romans, hope is for what is not seen yet, and is held with patience.
what a scholar hears: Paul sets hope inside the labor pains of creation and ties it to the resurrection; it is trust in a promise, not a forecast.
